title: Banned from Harvard
hookLine: the Divinity School Address so upset the clergy that, the usual account goes, Harvard didn't ask him back for a long time

cards: A guest is invited to speak to a class of young men about to become ministers. He's polite, soft-spoken, a former minister himself.
And in long, beautiful sentences he tells the room that the churches they're about to serve have lost touch with the living soul. Then he goes home. The reaction does not stay in the room.
It goes into print, sharply. And by the usual account, Harvard does not ask Ralph Waldo Emerson back to speak for a long, long time.

teach.h: MADE TOO MUCH OF THE PERSON.
teach.b: First, what he said. Yesterday's snowstorm was one part of this same talk.
The deeper part was Emerson's charge that the churches had made too much of the person of Jesus, and too little of the divine life Jesus pointed to in every soul.

His advice to the young ministers, in his own words: "go alone; to refuse the good models, even those which are sacred in the imagination of men, and dare to love God without mediator or veil." Second, why it hurt.
For the ministers and professors in that room, Jesus was not a model to set aside.

teach.h: TO THEM, THE CENTER OF THE FAITH.
teach.b: He was the center of the faith, the one through whom God is known. Their alarm was sincere, and it came from what they loved. A scholar who had taught at the school answered in print, calling it a new form of unbelief.
Third, what Emerson did next. Almost nothing. He didn't publish a reply.
When a friend and colleague wrote asking him to defend his views, Emerson answered that he couldn't give arguments for them.

teach.h: NO ARGUMENTS, ONLY WHAT HE SAW.
teach.b: He could only say what he saw. Fourth, the lesson anyone can take, whichever side of that room they'd have sat on. Saying a true thing, as you see it, can cost you an invitation, or a friendship.
Emerson stayed gentle in manner while saying something hard in substance.
True and kind don't always arrive together. But you can try to keep them in the same sentence.

how: Emerson's Divinity School Address is often read as a case study in speaking an unpopular conviction: what he said, how sincerely his hearers objected, and how he declined to argue back.

o: what Emerson's hard talk at Harvard cost him, by the usual account
Emerson's choice to refuse an honor Harvard offered him

games.q: you're Emerson. your talk has caused an uproar, and a friend writes asking you to defend it with arguments. what do you do?
o: say you have no arguments, only what you see.
games.why: he told his friend he couldn't give arguments for his views. he could only say what he saw, and he left it there.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've been holding something back from, a worry, a disagreement, a piece of honest feedback, and find the true thing in as few words as you can.
Then picture them and ask how you'd say it if you wanted them to hear it, not just to have said it. Let the words soften without going false.

wordCard.voice: Banned from Harvard. The usual account of what Emerson's Divinity School Address cost him: a sincere uproar, a sharp reply in print, and a long time before he was asked back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: true and kind. Hard in substance and gentle in manner, both at once. See you tomorrow.
